Your task is to perform matrix operations using the appropriate Pandas, NumPy, IPython, Jupyter, or scientific-Python technique. Do not hard-code the sample answer. Your program must work for every valid input satisfying the constraints.

Additional requirements: preserve the required ordering; handle all records; use the operation specified in the statement; and do not modify unrelated data.

Sample Input

recordCount = 10
values = [90, 6, 13, 20, 27, 34, 41, 48, 55, 62]
secondaryValues = [58, 63, 68, 73, 78, 83, 5, 10, 15, 20]
operationVariant = 2

Sample Output

The required result after applying the stated perform matrix operations operation.
The output must contain exactly the requested values, rows, shape, or table.
Full challenge details

For the hidden tests, recordCount may range from 1 to 100,000. Values may include negative numbers, zero, repeated values, and boundary cases whenever the operation permits them. When the task concerns tabular data, column and index order must follow the rules in the statement. When the task concerns arrays, preserve NumPy's specified shape and axis semantics.

Concept

@ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication - row-by-column dot products - as opposed to *, which multiplies elementwise; mixing the two up is one of the most common NumPy bugs for anyone coming from a purely elementwise mental model.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [90, 6, 13, 20, 27, 34, 41, 48, 55, 62]
secondary = [58, 63, 68, 73, 78, 83, 5, 10, 15, 20]
a = np.array(values)
b = np.array(secondary)
size = min(len(a), len(b))
r = 1
for cand in range(2, size + 1):
    if size % cand == 0:
        r = cand
        break
ma = a[:size].reshape(r, -1)
mb = b[:size].reshape(-1, r)
print(ma)
print(mb)
print(ma @ mb)

Output

[[90  6 13 20 27]
 [34 41 48 55 62]]
[[58 63]
 [68 73]
 [78 83]
 [ 5 10]
 [15 20]]
[[ 7147  7927]
 [ 9709 10909]]

Your task is to perform matrix operations using the appropriate Pandas, NumPy, IPython, Jupyter, or scientific-Python technique. Do not hard-code the sample answer. Your program must work for every valid input satisfying the constraints.

Additional requirements: preserve the required ordering; handle all records; use the operation specified in the statement; and do not modify unrelated data.

Sample Input

recordCount = 8
values = [78, 85, 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36]
secondaryValues = [2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37]
operationVariant = 5

Sample Output

The required result after applying the stated perform matrix operations operation.
The output must contain exactly the requested values, rows, shape, or table.
Full challenge details

For the hidden tests, recordCount may range from 1 to 100,000. Values may include negative numbers, zero, repeated values, and boundary cases whenever the operation permits them. When the task concerns tabular data, column and index order must follow the rules in the statement. When the task concerns arrays, preserve NumPy's specified shape and axis semantics.

Concept

@ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication - row-by-column dot products - as opposed to *, which multiplies elementwise; mixing the two up is one of the most common NumPy bugs for anyone coming from a purely elementwise mental model.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [78, 85, 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36]
secondary = [2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, 37]
a = np.array(values)
b = np.array(secondary)
size = min(len(a), len(b))
r = 1
for cand in range(2, size + 1):
    if size % cand == 0:
        r = cand
        break
ma = a[:size].reshape(r, -1)
mb = b[:size].reshape(-1, r)
print(ma)
print(mb)
print(ma @ mb)

Output

[[78 85  1  8]
 [15 22 29 36]]
[[ 2  7]
 [12 17]
 [22 27]
 [32 37]]
[[1454 2314]
 [2084 2594]]

Sample Input

Full challenge details

When the task concerns tabular data, column and index order must follow the rules in the statement. When the task concerns arrays, preserve NumPy's specified shape and axis semantics.

Concept

@ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication - row-by-column dot products - as opposed to *, which multiplies elementwise; mixing the two up is one of the most common NumPy bugs for anyone coming from a purely elementwise mental model.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [54, 61, 68, 75, 82, 89, 5, 12, 19, 26]
secondary = [56, 61, 66, 71, 76, 81, 3, 8, 13, 18]
a = np.array(values)
b = np.array(secondary)
size = min(len(a), len(b))
r = 1
for cand in range(2, size + 1):
    if size % cand == 0:
        r = cand
        break
ma = a[:size].reshape(r, -1)
mb = b[:size].reshape(-1, r)
print(ma)
print(mb)
print(ma @ mb)

Full challenge details

When the task concerns tabular data, column and index order must follow the rules in the statement. When the task concerns arrays, preserve NumPy's specified shape and axis semantics.

Concept

@ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication - row-by-column dot products - as opposed to *, which multiplies elementwise; mixing the two up is one of the most common NumPy bugs for anyone coming from a purely elementwise mental model.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [30, 37, 44, 51, 58, 65]
secondary = [27, 32, 37, 42, 47, 52]
a = np.array(values)
b = np.array(secondary)
size = min(len(a), len(b))
r = 1
for cand in range(2, size + 1):
    if size % cand == 0:
        r = cand
        break
ma = a[:size].reshape(r, -1)
mb = b[:size].reshape(-1, r)
print(ma)
print(mb)
print(ma @ mb)

Output

[[30 37 44]
 [51 58 65]]
[[27 32]
 [37 42]
 [47 52]]
[[4247 4802]
 [6578 7448]]

Concept

@ (or np.matmul) performs true matrix multiplication - row-by-column dot products - as opposed to *, which multiplies elementwise; mixing the two up is one of the most common NumPy bugs for anyone coming from a purely elementwise mental model.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [18, 25, 32, 39, 46, 53, 60, 67, 74, 81]
secondary = [54, 59, 64, 69, 74, 79, 1, 6, 11, 16]

b = np.array(secondary)
size = min(len(a), len(b))
r = 1
for cand in range(2, size + 1):
    if size % cand == 0:
        r = cand
        break
ma = a[:size].reshape(r, -1)
mb = b[:size].reshape(-1, r)
print(ma)
print(mb)
print(ma @ mb)

You are given a dataset representing daily sales analyzer. The data contains records from several days or entities, and the statement may include repeated categories, missing values, non-default indexes, or multiple related tables depending on the operation being tested.

Your task is to index a matrix using the appropriate Pandas, NumPy, IPython, Jupyter, or scientific-Python technique. Do not hard-code the sample answer. Your program must work for every valid input satisfying the constraints.

Additional requirements: preserve the required ordering; handle all records; use the operation specified in the statement; and do not modify unrelated data.

Sample Input

recordCount = 7
values = [89, 5, 12, 19, 26, 33, 40]
secondaryValues = [19, 24, 29, 34, 39, 44, 49]
operationVariant = 3

Sample Output

The required result after applying the stated index a matrix operation.
The output must contain exactly the requested values, rows, shape, or table.
Full challenge details

For the hidden tests, recordCount may range from 1 to 100,000. Values may include negative numbers, zero, repeated values, and boundary cases whenever the operation permits them. When the task concerns tabular data, column and index order must follow the rules in the statement. When the task concerns arrays, preserve NumPy's specified shape and axis semantics.

Concept

For a 2-D array, matrix[i, j] accesses the element at row i, column j directly with a single comma-separated index, rather than the nested matrix[i][j] style a list of lists would require.

Show solution
import numpy as np

values = [89, 5, 12, 19, 26, 33, 40]
a = np.array(values)
m = a.reshape(7, -1)
print(m)
print(m[1, min(1, m.shape[1]-1)])

Output

[[89]
 [ 5]
 [12]
 [19]
 [26]
 [33]
 [40]]
5

The required result after applying the stated iterate over rows operation.

Problem 009

recordCount = 7

The required result after applying the stated iterate over elements operation.

Concept
